entries.title: Measles Outbreaks Are Forcing Immunocompromised Kids to Make Impossible Choices
entries.summary: With the risk of infection rising, parents and young adults are facing agonizing choices about being out in public as school starts back up.
entries.content:
As students head back to school, parents have all the usual worries about their kids, like remembering to pack lunch and making it to the bus stop on time. But parents of immunocompromised kids have a new one: How to deal with the resurgence of measles.

Cases of the highly transmissible disease have reached a 35-year high in the US, with nearly 3,000 confirmed infections in 2026 so far. The first two measles-related deaths of the year were recorded in Pennsylvania, right as the school year is getting going. With vaccination rates dropping across the country, parents of kids who aren’t able to get vaccinated or don’t mount a strong enough immune response due to weakened immune systems are weighing whether it’s safe enough to go to school.

Victoria Schiano, national community engagement coordinator for Little Lobbyists, a nonprofit that advocates for children with complex medical needs and disabilities, says the return of measles is “absolutely terrifying.”

While it’s not known exactly how many US children have compromised immune systems, a study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that 2.6 percent of children are immunocompromised. Immune deficiencies can have genetic causes or secondary reasons, such as chemotherapy for cancer treatment.

Schiano’s kid is among them. Her 10-year-old has mitochondrial disease. The family lives in Chester County, Pennsylvania, which has the second-highest number of measles cases in the state right now. Schiano has been closely monitoring the vaccination rates in her son’s school district, which have dipped below the 95 percent threshold needed for community protection against measles. Measles is breaking through in places where vaccination has dropped below that threshold. In neighboring Lancaster County, for example, just 87.6 percent of kindergartners are fully vaccinated against measles and 83.3 percent of seventh graders are.

Her son can’t be vaccinated, and he receives weekly infusions of immunoglobulin—concentrated antibodies from donated human blood plasma—to help his body fight infections.

“Measles is dangerous for anyone, but for him, this absolutely could be life or death,” she says.

The virus can cause severe, life-threatening complications such as pneumonia and brain swelling. Measles can also wipe out the body’s memory of past infections—a phenomenon known as immune amnesia—leaving people susceptible to other diseases.

Her son already wears a mask and uses a plexiglass screen at school, and the family is diligent about handwashing. Now, Schiano says they’ve had to make the difficult decision to limit her son’s time with friends and after-school activities like karate. She says it’s hard as a parent to balance his quality of life with his safety.

“He just wants to play and to do all the things that he sees other kids doing,” she says.

Her son did online school for a time during Covid-19, and she says she’s prepared to take him out of school if there’s even one confirmed measles case. That comes with a different set of risks, though. During the pandemic, remote learning was associated with an increase in social isolation and behavioral and mental health issues among students.

Amalia, a parent in South Carolina who asked to go by a pseudonym for privacy reasons, has already chosen to keep her 16-year-old son home this year and do online schooling due to concerns about measles. Her son has immunoglobulin A deficiency, in which the body doesn’t produce enough of an antibody found in mucous membranes, body fluids, and digestive tracts that help fend off germs.

“Even if there’s just a flu going around, he gets sicker than the average kid will,” she says.

Her son was able to get the measles vaccine, but doctors monitor his antibody levels regularly to check for waning immunity.

She lives in Spartanburg County, where measles broke out earlier this year and caused nearly 1,000 cases and 21 hospitalizations. About 91 percent of those cases were among children and teens, and most were among those who were not fully vaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. Even though there was a 94 percent increase in the number of vaccines administered during the outbreak in Spartanburg County compared to the year before, she still wasn’t comfortable sending her son back to school.

“Covid happened, and then measles happened, and we just feel like it's not going to be the last time,” she says. “If it's not measles, it's going to be something else because rates for other vaccines have fallen, too.”

Before this year, her son shared a classroom with other students who have special accommodations. But outside of that setting, Amalia says it has been difficult for him to make friends because of his medical condition. She says it’s hard to talk to other parents about vaccination status because it can be such a hot-button issue. The family is thinking about moving because of what she views as an anti-vaccination sentiment in the community as well as “hostility” toward masking that she’s encountered.

“Some people don't want to take ownership of the responsibility of public health,” she says. “I think it's something we're supposed to share across humanity. It's not supposed to be carried by one person.”

Cortney, another South Carolina parent of an immunocompromised kid, says the state’s measles outbreak was highly concerning because the family needed to travel near the epicenter for medical appointments. Whereas before they might stop in town to eat lunch or do some shopping, they ended any unnecessary stops. “We planned to drive directly into that county, we go only to the doctor, and we leave,” Cortney says.

Her 17-year-old daughter Grace’s condition means that rhinovirus—the cause of the common cold—led to her getting hospitalized. During Covid, Grace and her brother were homeschooled, and that is something mother and daughter considered again for Grace’s senior year.

“At the end of the semester, we're going to reevaluate and see where things are,” Grace says.

Even though she is immunocompromised, Grace doesn’t wear a mask at school because of fear of being bullied. Cortney says her family’s preference would be to mask while in public, but she’s concerned about being ostracized. “You worry that your family could be targeted,” she says. “It’s unfortunate that we have to think about that.”

entries.title: The 6 Best Monitors That Actually Work Well With Macs
entries.summary: Macs are fantastic computers, but you’ll need one of these great displays to complete your work-from-home setup.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

The Mac Mini is back. And so is the Mac Studio. They’ve been nearly impossible to buy for most of 2026 thanks to the rising demand for running AI models locally. Prices have risen, yes, but when new models go on sale in late September, they’ll finally be out in the wild. And with that, you’ll want a decent monitor to match.

Whether you need something basic or you're a content creator looking for a high-end display, one of these monitors I’ve tested below should do the trick. They’ll work with any Mac, not just the Mac Mini.

Be sure to check our Best Apple Desktops, Best MacBooks, Best Monitors, Best Monitor Arms, and Best Gaming Monitors guides for more.

Updated September 2026: I’ve oriented this guide toward monitors that work with any type of Mac (not just a Mac Mini), and I’ve added a number of monitors I recently tested, such as the BenQ MQ270S, Apple Studio Display XDR, and Asus ProArt 27 QD-OLED. I’ve also added some recommended new monitor arms from my recent batch of testing.

What to Look For in a Mac Monitor

Just about any monitor can work with a Mac. It doesn’t need to be made by Apple or have any official certification. There’s a case to be made for using a cheap 1080p monitor, but most Mac users will want something a bit more premium. As you can see from options like the Dell 27 Plus 4K, that doesn’t have to mean overly expensive. Either way, here are the four elements to consider when shopping for a good monitor to go with your Mac.

Size and resolution: 27- and 32-inch monitors are the most common sizes these days, but there are larger options. I would also consider a 34-inch ultrawide monitor if you like the wider 21:9 aspect ratio with the curved shape. With Apple, resolution is king. There's a reason it invests so much in high pixel density for every screen it sells, even in midrange options like the MacBook Air. Pixel density is what gives a screen its sharpness, and you need a lot more pixels when they're stretched across a large external monitor. If you want to keep fidelity up, I wouldn’t buy anything less than 4K, and bumping up to 5K or 6K on a 32-inch monitor can be helpful. Read more to learn the details on the funky way macOS handles resolutions and scaling. You should also consider the refresh rate: a 120-Hz refresh rate is what the MacBook Pro supports, offering smoother animation, especially in games.

Adjustability: Apple monitors and iMacs aren’t exactly known for adjustability. They often have none at all, and cost more when they do. That isn’t the best for your posture and ergonomics. Famously, the discontinued Pro Display XDR charged an extra $1,000 for a Pro Stand with proper adjustability (now a $400 add-on for the newer Studio Display XDR). For ergonomics, the top of the screen you're working on should be as close to eye level as possible, and that ranges depending on someone’s height. If a monitor doesn’t have height adjustability, you’ll need a separate monitor stand or arm. Beyond height adjustment, many monitors also have stands that can swivel, tilt, and rotate, all of which matter when using multiple monitors. This is also needed if you want to use a second monitor vertically, which has become increasingly popular.

Ports: Even the cheapest monitors will always have HDMI, which is all you need to connect directly to a Mac Mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro, or MacBook Pro. Some monitors have USB-C that supports video, which will let you connect to one of a Mac’s Thunderbolt ports. The Mac Mini comes with three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an Ethernet jack. The Mac Mini Pro model has the same ports, except three of them support faster Thunderbolt 5 instead of 4. You’ll need to use at least one of these Thunderbolt ports to connect more than one external monitor. These monitors also tend to have other ports, such as USB-A. These can be useful, as the Mac Mini doesn't have any on its own.

Image quality: Apple prides itself on the image quality of its Macs, so in the case of the Mac Mini, you’ll likely want to get something worthy of your Mac. This is especially important for content creators, photographers, and designers. So, consider a monitor’s brightness, color accuracy, color coverage, and contrast. While some IPS displays offer decent color and contrast, mini-LED or OLED displays will guarantee better image quality. These also have significantly higher peak brightness in HDR content, which really brings games and movies to life.

How Many Monitors Can a Mac Mini Support?

The latest Mac Mini with the M6 chip can support up to three external displays, using the three Thunderbolt ports or one HDMI port on the back. Regardless of the resolution (up to 8K) or refresh rate (up to 240 Hz), if you're just plugging in a single monitor, any one of these ports will do. Use whichever your monitor has or whichever is the most convenient. But when you need multiple displays, that's where things get complicated. Here's a table explaining the differences.

Mac Mini Model One Display Two Displays Three Displays
M6 Up to one 8K display at 50 Hz or 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz and one display up to 5K at 60 Hz (using Thunderbolt) or 4K at 60 Hz (using HDMI) Up to two 6K displays at 60 Hz or 4K at 165 Hz and third display up to 5K at 60 Hz (using Thunderbolt) or 4K at 60 Hz (using HDMI)
M5 Pro Up to one 8K display at 50 Hz or 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz and one display up to 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 200 Hz Up to three 6K displays at 60 Hz or 4K at 165 Hz
M4 Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 4K display at 240 Hz Up to one 6K display at 60 Hz and one display at 4K at 144 Hz Up to two 6K displays at 60 Hz and one 5K at 60 Hz (using Thunderbolt) or 4K at 60 Hz (using HDMI)
M4 Pro Up to one 8K at 60 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz and one 6K at 60 Hz or 4K at 144 Hz Up to three 6K displays at 60 Hz or three 4K displays at 144 Hz
M2 Up to one 6K display at 60 Hz or 4K at 60 Hz Up to one 6K display at 60 Hz and 5K display at 60 Hz (using Thunderbolt) or 4K at 60 Hz (using HDMI) Not supported
M2 Pro Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz Up to two displays at 6K at 60 Hz or one display at 4K at 144Hz Up to two 6K displays at 60 Hz and one display at 4K at 60 Hz
M1 4K display at 60 Hz One 6K and one 4K at 60 Hz Not supported

Why Macs Don't Run 4K Resolutions Natively

When you plug in an external 4K monitor to a Mac of any kind, it will look good. The icons, text, and UI elements look sharp and not overly small. But open up the Display menu in System Settings, and you'll find that it’s not actually rendering at the full resolution of 3840 x 2160. Instead, it'll default to a much lower resolution to achieve that scaling. In fact, this happens even on the integrated display of a MacBook Air, which defaults to 1470 x 956 instead of the native 2560 x 1664. No doubt, this is one reason macOS defaults to hiding the list of resolutions and instead just asks the user how large they want the text to appear.

I won’t get into the rather complex reasoning behind this, but know this: the resolution you see in the macOS display settings doesn't appear to be that resolution. That's what Apple's Retina Display branding is all about: preserving clarity. And when you plug in an external monitor, macOS will maintain that priority of clarity at the expense of native resolution.

That said, there are a few resolutions and screen sizes that are best optimized for macOS’ proclivities. Namely, it's 27-inch monitors with a 5K resolution (5120 x 2880), which gives you exactly twice the resolution of 1440p and produces an extremely sharp image without messing up the scaling. That doesn't mean 4K monitors won't work or aren't worth the money; just don't expect things to work exactly how they do when connected to Windows.

Mac Mini or iMac?

If you haven’t already bought your Mac Mini, you might be wondering if it's a better deal than the iMac. After all, both are desktop Macs with similar specs and performance. The M6 Mac Mini starts at $899, which gets you 16 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage. The M4 iMac, on the other hand, costs $1,499. It has an older processor, but comes with the same memory and storage, a built-in 24-inch display with 4480 x 2520 (4.5K) resolution, a 12-megapixel webcam, a mouse, a keyboard, and some decent speakers. For the $600 difference, you either get a computer with a newer processor but no display or accessories, or an all-in-one that's ready out of the box.

It's hard to quantify, though, as there aren't any 4.5K monitors out there. The 24-inch monitor size has largely disappeared, except for ultra-budget displays or professional esports gaming monitors. However, you can certainly buy a quality 27-inch 4K monitor for less than $500 (and a 5K variant for not much more), with money left over to add on peripherals such as a webcam or computer speakers. So, in terms of cost savings, grabbing the Mac Mini is a smart move. You're paying extra for the iMac’s convenience of it being an all-in-one system.

More Great Mac Accessories

Kit out your Mac with these other accessories, and make sure to check out our Best Mac Accessories guide for more.

Satechi Mac Mini M4 Hub Stand for $75: Very few products are designed specifically for the Mac Mini, which is what makes this USB hub and stand from Satechi so special. It gives you forward-facing USB-A ports and an SD card slot, plus an enclosure for an NVMe SSD drive to expand a Mac Mini's integrated storage.

Herman Miller Flo Single Monitor Arm for $305: You’d better have a nice monitor if you’re even considering this monitor arm, which is one of the most expensive I’ve ever seen. But after testing it, I have to say I was impressed by what it offers. Most monitor arms share a lot in common, but this one uses an innovative mechanism that attaches the back of the screen in an entirely different way, resulting in a remarkably smooth sense of motion. It’s not for everyone, but it definitely won me over.

Logitech MX Master 4 for $120: The Logitech MX Master mouse has been a mainstay on the desks of Mac users who are serious about productivity and comfort. The latest version isn’t a major overhaul, but it makes tweaks to modernize the design, using better materials, haptics, and a new thumb rest button. But everything that made the MX Master series so great is still here.

BenQ Ergo Arm for $150: This is my favorite monitor arm. I’ve tested a bunch recently, and I really like the complete package of the Ergo Arm. The white color is nice, and while it’s extremely sturdy and can handle just about any monitor (no matter how large), it doesn’t feel as clunky as some other monitor arms I’ve tested. Extra features like the included reinforcement plate to prevent damage to your desk also sweeten the deal.

Harber London Leather Desk Mat for $239: If you’re looking to upgrade the look and feel of your desk and complement your Mac Mini, a desk mat goes a long way. It’ll endure some wear and tear on your desk, but this high-end leather option from Harber London has the quality to last many years of use. And yes, it’s gorgeous.

Hemudu Monitor Stands for $30: If your monitor doesn’t have proper height adjustment, elevating it is key to keeping it at eye level. There are tons of different options out there, but this affordable monitor stand is especially nice for those setting up two monitors side by side.

entries.title: ICE Wants to Know Who Bought a Certain Green Beanie From REI in the Last 2 Years
entries.summary: Homeland Security Investigations agents hit the outdoor retailer with a controversial subpoena as part of a dragnet search for the identities of protesters who entered a Minnesota church in March.
entries.content:
Did you buy a beanie from REI recently? The Department of Homeland Security might be looking for you.

New court filings allege that Homeland Security Investigations agents subpoenaed the outdoor retailer in March, requesting the transaction information for “all persons” in the greater Minneapolis-St. Paul area who had purchased a specific type of dark green beanie from the company since 2024. REI did not respond to questions about whether it had complied with the request and, if so, how many people are affected.

The filings are part of a broader lawsuit by the federal government against 39 people who attended an ICE protest at a church whose pastor also worked as an acting ICE field office director. Both protesters and journalists who were attempting to cover the event, including former CNN host Don Lemon, are now defendants.

The subpoena to REI was one of 92 sent as part of HSI’s investigation into the defendants, according to the court filings. Other recipients included social media companies, airlines, telecom providers, a car rental company, and a state employment agency. At least one subpoena sent to an unnamed airline, the filings allege, asked not only for information about a defendant’s past flights, but also requested that the airline give HSI a “lookout notification” about the defendant’s travel in the future. DHS declined to comment. The US Attorney’s Office in Minnesota, which is litigating the case on behalf of the government, did not respond questions about why it was necessary to identify everyone in Minnesota who purchased the beanie from REI, or why it specifically targeted REI customers, since the beanie is sold on other platforms as well.

The subpoenas sent by HSI agents are also known as 1509 customs summons, and are meant to be used to request information related to imports and exports. However, since the start of the Trump administration, WIRED and other news outlets have reported on DHS’s attempts to unmask online critics using the legal tool, which can be sent without the oversight of a judge or a jury.

“It's flat-out absurd for DHS to demand REI search two years of customer data as part of Trump’s campaign against the people of Minneapolis,” US senator Ron Wyden of Oregon tells WIRED. “Customs summonses only allow DHS to request information directly related to compliance with customs laws, not to conduct unending fishing expeditions into the lives of people critical of Donald Trump.”

The total number of 1509 summonses that have been sent since the start of the Trump administration—and how many people have had their personal information guzzled up by DHS as a result—is unknown. Companies that receive these types of subpoenas are typically asked to keep their existence a secret. When the public has gotten a glimpse of them, it's usually because the target has contested it in court, either because the recipient company ignored the request for silence and notified the target, or because the target discovered it after the fact.

According to a recent letter written by Wyden and Representative Pramila Jayapal, big tech companies will sometimes ignore the government's request for silence when not legally required, but other companies in more heavily regulated sectors have told Congress that they've complied because of fear of regulatory retaliation.

Court filings, internal DHS documents, and companies’ own public statements show that companies have responded to recent customs summons in different ways.

Attorneys for Georgia Fort, a journalist and one of the defendants in the Minnesota case, wrote in a court filing that they were “stunned” when they realized that the government had obtained logs detailing six months’ of Fort’s calls and text messages from T-Mobile after the government sent a customs summons to the telecom provider. The attorneys allege that Fort was never notified by either T-Mobile nor the government.

“We take our responsibility to protect customers’ privacy and personal information very seriously,” says a T-Mobile spokesperson, who also said the company does not comment on specific legal requests. “Our team carefully reviews government demands for customer information and responds in accordance with the law.”

In the same filing, the attorneys said that Google refused to comply with a customs summons requesting information about Fort’s YouTube viewers and subscribers. A Google spokesperson says that the company reviews each government request for lawfulness and that Google will try to narrow requests or outright reject them when it believes the request is too broad.

Reddit recently announced that during the last half of 2025, it received DHS administrative subpoenas seeking information about 11 different Reddit accounts that made critical posts about ICE actions. After Reddit objected to them on First Amendment grounds, the company said, the agency withdrew them.

“Privacy is central to how Reddit operates, and we take our commitment to protecting it seriously,” says Ben Lee, Reddit’s outgoing chief legal officer. “We routinely push back on law enforcement requests and stand up for users who are exercising their First Amendment rights.”

Meta also pushed back against at least one customs summons, according to internal DHS correspondence obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Meta declined WIRED’s request to comment.

“I think DHS has proved time and time again that they can’t be trusted as the stewards of applying this law correctly,” says Mario Trujillo, a senior staff attorney at the EFF who has been tracking DHS subpoenas sent to tech companies. Congress could pass a law that would restrict how the agency used 1509 customs summons, or add penalties when they are misused, but until then companies and their customers are on their own.

entries.title: AI Use in the Job Market Is Creating an Infinite Doom Loop
entries.summary: Job seekers are trying to game the application process using AI. It’s not working, and not for the reasons you might think.
entries.content:
Jodi Beggs' résumé got dinged for being two pages long. She used her middle initial on one document but not another, which also cost her points. If she changed “percent” to the % sign, her score went up.

Beggs, a data scientist and job seeker, got this feedback from an online system that compares a job description with an applicant's materials to assess how well they match up. The most well known of these tools is Jobscan, though Beggs didn't say which one she tested.

“If my job is to please the robots,” Beggs says, “then even if I don't like AI-generated content, maybe the machines do.”

Jobscan and other apps like it work on the premise that hiring committees use AI to automatically rate and rank candidates in their applicant tracking system (ATS). Only the top 10 to 20 percent of applicants are considered. The bottom 80 might never see the light of day. That's the belief, anyway. To get on the short list, candidates must tailor the formatting of their CVs and cover letters and pack them with the right keywords to match what the ATS wants to see.

The problem is, this premise isn’t always correct. Automated ranking absolutely happens in some organizations, but in others, hiring is still managed personally by humans from start to finish.

The Curse of the Applicant Tracking System

At its most basic, an ATS collects job applications, helps hiring committees review them, and tracks applicants through the interviewing and hiring process. Some systems offer more, from onboarding management to automated AI screening interviews.

Daniel Chait, CEO of an ATS company called Greenhouse, says there's a lot of folklore about these tools, particularly from the job seeker side. No two ATSs are the same. The technology changes fast, so an AI tool inside an ATS might work one way today and a different way tomorrow. Whether an ATS uses AI at all depends on the exact product and which features a team pays for and uses.

Regardless, as long as applicants believe AI is involved, they'll still try to game it using their own AI.

To put the fate of your job search into the hands of a tool that says it can optimize for an ATS is a shaky proposition. One recruiter proved how even with atrocious Jobscan scores, she still got a dozen interviews and an offer. Consider, too, that Jobscan costs $30 to $50 per month. The company isn't exactly incentivized to get you off the job market.

Being in a low-fire, low-hire economy only makes matters worse. Job postings are scarce. Scams and ghost jobs are enough of a problem that some states are looking to write new laws to combat them.

Both job seekers and employers say they're experiencing a breakdown of trust. Candidates sink so much time into their search and hear nothing. Applying to jobs is a black box.

Some employers, meanwhile, say they receive hundreds of applications that look nearly identical. So they feed them into the AI rating system of their ATS to try and get some quick differentiation.

Chait says we're in an AI doom loop. “We've got this tragic situation where each side has a problem. They're using AI to solve their own problem, but in ways that make the problem worse. And so more AI use begets more AI use, to no one's benefit. The more it's happening, the worse it gets.”

Comparing Human Vetting to AI

I spoke with dozens of recruiters and HR managers, as well as small business owners who do their own hiring. Some admitted they use automated candidate ranking, and some were adamant that they do not. The division has nothing to do with the size of the organization or even the number of applicants received. It seems driven by philosophy and culture.

Kim Jones is vice president of human resources at Toshiba. “We have humans review every application,” she says. She doesn't mind applicants using AI to polish up their materials, but “it's not really going to help with getting through the ATS.” Culling applicants comes down to job requirements, salary expectations, and a few other factors, like whether the person would be a rehire.

Where she has seen unwanted AI usage is in the interviewing stage. “You hear the pause, maybe hear the typing, then they come up with a verbose answer,” Jones says.

Another company that relies more on humans than technology for hiring is Doist. It's a small, fully remote company that hires internationally, which means when they have an opening, they're flush with applications.

Nadia Vatalidis, head of people at the company, says her team experimented to see if ATS rankings could help. They took roles that had already been filled and fed in the job descriptions as well as all the applicant materials that they had saved from the hiring process. They wanted to know “what would happen if AI had to short-list the same batch of candidates and whether the folks we interviewed would show up in those same categories,” Vatalidis says. “In two instances that we tested, the person we hired wasn't in the short list.” She says there was overlap in who got an interview, but their new hires—people who were working out great after about six months—didn't make the cut.

Using AI Differently

When James Jacobsen started his job search five months ago, the amount of time he sank into searching and applying to jobs was equivalent to a full-time role. As a design professional, he knows AI can't match him when it comes to creativity, but he experiments with it heavily and knows it's a powerful tool for certain tasks. He used Claude and ChatGPT to polish up his application materials and make sure they were in line with the job description, but it wasn't moving the needle.

Instead of focusing only on his application materials, he started using Claude to streamline and track his job search from top to bottom. He instructed it to comb job listings, analyze descriptions, and log them. He devised an elaborate scoring system based on the type of work, seniority, and his salary requirements, which varied for in-person, hybrid, and remote roles. His AI assistant highlighted the top jobs he should apply to. When he rejected one, he added a note, so if the same position got reposted weeks later, his AI could immediately remind him why he wasn't interested. He spent less time searching to find more high-quality positions. He got a few bites but no offers.

He effectively built the opposite of an ATS—a tracking system for the job seeker.

He didn't stop there. Next, Jacobsen asked Claude and ChatGPT to critique his portfolio, resulting in a six-hour revamp. Two days later, he got a call from a prospective employer, but it still didn't result in an offer.

Chait says job candidates like Jacobsen are asking themselves how they can possibly put in more effort. “Doing more of the same isn't the answer,” he says.

“This is the first time I can remember when both sides are unhappy,” Chait says. “It's just not working.” For job seekers, “I'd say the answer is not just more spray-and-pray,” he says.

Spend time researching companies where you might want to work, Chait says, even if they aren't the first names that come to mind. Kim Jones of Toshiba mentioned that she almost never sees a cover letter anymore and says applicants stand out if they submit one. Networking is yet another underrated skill in today's job market.

Chait has one more message for job seekers, which is to remember: “It's not you; it’s the system, and it stinks.”

entries.title: What the Heck? Another Perfect Geometric Shape Has Been Detected on Saturn
entries.summary: The discovery adds to the planet’s history of strange atmospheric phenomena that scientists don’t full understand.
entries.content:
A team of astronomers discovered a strange polygonal atmospheric structure on Saturn near the planet’s south pole. This 10-sided shape, known as a decagon, joins one of the gas giant’s most famous features: a hexagon near the north pole that was first observed 44 years ago. Images of the new decagon were captured by the Hubble Space Telescope, and the discovery was recently published in the journal Science Advances.

The formations at both the north and south poles aren’t solid structures, like a wall or a rock formation. Saturn doesn’t even have a defined solid surface like Earth’s crust. If you were to descend through the atmosphere of the ringed planet, the pressure and density would progressively increase, but you would never reach a “ground” on which to land. Instead, what astronomers have witnessed are patterns formed by clouds, albeit very unusual ones.

Each side of the decagon measures approximately 16,800 kilometers, which is a few thousand miles longer than the diameter of Earth. Near the feature is a jet stream reaching speeds of 116 meters per second, or nearly 260 miles per hour. By way of comparison, a Category 5 hurricane—the most intense storm level possible on Earth—is defined by winds above 157 miles per hour. Interestingly, although the jet stream circulates at tremendous speed, the decagon pattern shifts at a mere 2.5 meters per second—less than 6 miles per hour.

The south pole feature appears to have formed recently. For decades, scientists have been searching for a counterpart to the famous northern hexagon. However, major missions that observed the planet have previously not been able to find an equivalent, long-lasting structure in the south. The search was further complicated because, due to Saturn’s tilt, its southern hemisphere was not clearly visible from Earth for many years.

The first clues of the decagon came from ground-based observations, some by amateur astronomers. As the images accumulated, it became evident that something strange was happening in Saturn’s southern cloud bands. Data from the Hubble Space Telescope made it possible to trace the pattern back to images taken in 2023. Monitoring continued, and by 2025 its 10 vertices had become much more clearly defined, confirming the presence of a new polygonal feature in the ringed planet’s atmosphere. Science, however, hasn’t settled on an explanation for how these structures came to be.

Various hypotheses have been proposed since the discovery of the north polar hexagon. One is that the polygons are the visible manifestations of enormous atmospheric waves confined by powerful jet streams. You can think of these as similar to ocean waves, which are not simply objects traveling across the ocean but rather disturbances propagating through the water.

A wave’s behavior changes depending on the space in which it moves and the boundaries it encounters. On Saturn, waves of atmospheric gases may be encountering jet streams that confine them, in a sense, like the edge of a beach. Except in this case, the “beach” wraps all the way around the planet.

Various other factors, such as Saturn’s rapid rotation, exact wind speeds, and variations in the currents, could all contribute to the distinct geometries of the shapes. A current that coils around the planet six times can form a hexagon; one that does so 10 times, a decagon. This is one of the more likely explanations for how an atmosphere without any solid structure can end up forming something that looks like a gigantic polygon, but there are still many unanswered questions.

We don’t know how deep these geometric figures extend, how long the new decagon might last, whether its appearance is related to Saturn’s seasons, and—most importantly—what sparked its formation in the first place. Researchers hope to find some answers by tracking the decagon’s evolution. To do so, they plan to continue observations with the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes and use more advanced atmospheric models to reconstruct possible conditions that could give rise to such a structure.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: Silicon Valley Is Having a ‘Hot Girl Renaissance’
entries.summary: A San Francisco “Hot List” is trying to buck stereotypes about dating in tech circles amid wider debates about the value of being perceived as attractive.
entries.content:
Since the dawn of Silicon Valley, there’s been a widespread perception that San Francisco is, put gently, not exactly a dating mecca.

The city famously has a skewed male-to-female ratio (per census data, there are about 105 men for every 100 women), and there’s a perception among many women that men who work in tech tend to have poor social and emotional skills and a lack of style—opting for Patagonia vests and Meta glasses rather than putting substantive effort into their appearance.

On August 31, however, Celeste Amadon, the founder of the AI-powered dating app Known, valiantly attempted to reverse that stereotype. In an X thread accompanied by a moody, upward-angled selfie, she announced that she and her team were compiling a list of “SF’s most dateable people,” titled “San Francisco’s Hot List.” She attached a link for people to nominate their single friends according to criteria like “ambition,” “accomplishment,” “reputation,” and “aura.”

The post was skewered online by many in and outside of the tech scene, with some referring to it as “cringe” or mocking the lack of eligible singles in San Francisco: “The solution to dating in SF is to leave SF,” posted one female founder. But it was an extremely effective bit of marketing for Known, garnering more than 15,000 submissions 24 hours after the tweet was posted, according to Amadon. It was also an effective piece of counter-propaganda to the stereotype of San Franciscans, officially heralding that San Francisco Is Hot.

“Not to be cheesy, but I think the SF dating scene deserves some defending,” Amadon tells WIRED. “It gets so much flak for being a place where it’s hard to meet people, but there are many people who are super eligible in not just their physical attractiveness but in their holistic dateability.”

Known’s Hot List is part of a broader conversation focused on the general attractiveness of the San Francisco populace—and why some locals seem to be placing more importance on being perceived as hot.

Last summer, two women who work in tech—Madison Kanna (who is on the Hot List) and Cat Orman—threw an “enforced ratio” party at a Tesla showroom in the city, ensuring that there were as many women as men. The invite stipulated that the vibe would be “unapologetically feminine and fun” and that “​Patagonia vests will be turned away at the door.” On August 28, Mantis Biotech startup founder Georgia Witchel posted an X thread titled “Tech Is Having a Hot Girl Renaissance.” In the thread, Witchel describes how social media has been deluged with “young, attractive women taking tastefully slutty duck-faced mirror selfies” to promote their startups, citing Known and the insurance company Corgi as examples.

Witchel says her argument is not so much that she objects to young women using their attractiveness as a marketing strategy—it's more to explain how and why it has emerged as a marketing strategy to begin with, telling WIRED the trend is a result of “a renaissance of sales culture in SF.”

Throughout much of Silicon Valley, software marketing was “nerds selling to other nerds,” she says—but with the emergence of vibe coding, the barrier to entry for the industry has gotten lower, and the standards for marketing a product higher. “The fact that you are able to build a complicated product is not enough to give you the leeway of not being charismatic,” says Witchel. “People are recognizing that.”

When reached for comment, Brooke LeBlanc, head of community at Corgi, who Witchel cites in her thread, referred WIRED to an X post. “My mom just heard about the hot girl in tech renaissance and she’s absolutely thrilled by the news,” she wrote. “No one in my family from Georgia can believe that it’s breaking news for a woman to care about how she looks.”

Amadon says the Hot List has “minimal” connection to Witchel’s thread, but she understands why Known’s marketing “draws interest” (though she notes that X specifically is “not a primary marketing channel” for the app). She concedes that the list was intended to capitalize on the discussion and create “positive discourse” around dating in San Francisco.

And it’s working: On September 1, Known posted the first round of Hot Listers, including LeBlanc and startup founders like Jasper Carmichael-Jack, the CEO of the AI-driven company Artisan. There was nary a Patagonia vest in the bunch.

entries.summary: Save on Foreo favorites, including LUNA cleansing brushes, BEAR microcurrent devices, and masks and accessories to level up your daily skincare routine at home.
entries.content:
Beauty tool brand Foreo was launched by founder Filip Sedic in 2013, inspired by his wife’s facial brush, which he considered too abrasive and unsanitary. Since then, the Swedish brand has built a reputation for gentle, hygienic beauty tools across skincare, haircare, oral care, and eye care. More recently, the company has expanded into hair removal with IPL at-home devices like the Peach 2 Pro Max.

I’m currently testing the FAQ 202 Plus, Foreo’s latest LED mask, which features 634 LED lights and eight wavelengths: near-infrared, red, blue, green, orange, yellow, purple, and cyan. I’m also testing the Flip Play, an LED hairbrush for all hair types designed to reduce breakage, soothe the scalp, and stimulate hair follicles. I’m only in my first week of testing both devices, but I’ll report back soon. So far, both have been easy to use and simple to incorporate into my nighttime routine; the Flip Play brushes like a compact silicone detangler. In the meantime, here are some Foreo promo codes and deals if you’re considering splurging on a device.

30% Off Foreo LUNA 3 Plus: Heated Cleansing and Microcurrent in one Device

I haven’t tested the Foreo Luna 3 Plus myself, but it’s one of the brand’s bestsellers—and it’s 29% off (no Foreo promo code needed!). The heated device doubles as a facial cleanser and massager, with added microcurrent treatments. Its silicone build is more hygienic and bacteria-resistant than nylon brushes, and it offers 16 intensity levels to remove makeup and oil, loosen pores for a deeper clean, firm and lift the skin, and relax facial muscles. If you’re in the market for a multipurpose facial cleansing device, this deal makes a strong case for Foreo, especially with an included two-year warranty.

Foreo BEAR: Get 25% Off the Full Facial Workout Device

The Foreo Bear, like the Luna 3 Plus, includes microcurrent technology but is designed to prioritize it. The seasonal 25% Foreo discount makes it even more appealing value-wise. It’s made from the same bacteria-resistant silicone as the Luna and features 10 microcurrent intensity levels, plus guided treatments via the app. It requires a conductive serum or gel; Foreo’s Supercharged Serum 2.0 is one option, but it’s not required. Battery life is strong, offering up to 90 uses per USB charge. It’s available in bright fuchsia or mint, and it comes with a travel pouch for portability.

Foreo UFO 2 Deal: 29% Off 5-in-1 Spa Facials

The UFO 2 is a 5-in-1 facial device that is more affordable than both the Bear and the Luna 3 Plus. And it’s even cheaper right now with a 29% limited-time discount (with no Foreo promo code needed). Expect thermotherapy, cryotherapy, LED light, and T-sonic pulsations. The T-sonic pulses deliver low-frequency massage to ease facial and neck tension and support better blood flow. The UFO 2 also uses LED technology alongside hot and cold sonic waves to stimulate skin cells and enhance the absorption of skincare products. While I haven’t personally tested this device myself, Foreo’s track record with facial tools makes me eager to give this one a try.
